citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **formal power series over $R$** is a coefficient function $a:\mathbb N\to R$, written

$$f=\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n,$$

and $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ is the set of all such functions. The symbol $x$ is an indeterminate. The notation asserts no analytic convergence and no value of $x$ is being chosen.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, the **coefficient-extraction functional** is evaluation at $n$:

$$[x^n]f:=a_n.$$

Define zero and one coefficientwise, put $[x^n](f+g)=[x^n]f+[x^n]g$, and define the Cauchy product by

$$[x^n](fg)=\sum_{i+j=n}[x^i]f\,[x^j]g=\sum_{i=0}^{n}[x^i]f\,[x^{n-i}]g.$$

The last sum is finite, including when $n=0$. The constant $r\in R$ denotes the series with coefficient $r$ at $0$ and $0$ elsewhere. The series $x$ has coefficient $1$ at $1$ and $0$ elsewhere. Thus $x^0=1$, and $x^n$ is supported at $n$.

The finitely supported coefficient functions form the polynomial part of $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$. Under the coefficient-function definition of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], a polynomial is therefore the same data as a finitely supported formal series; the next theorem verifies that this identification respects the ring operations.

For every commutative ring $R$, the coefficientwise sum and Cauchy product make $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ a commutative ring. The coefficientwise inclusion

$$j:R[x]\longrightarrow R\llbracket x\rrbracket$$

is an injective unital ring homomorphism, and its image is exactly the finitely supported formal series.

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]). An element $a \in R$ is a **zero divisor**
when

$$a \ne 0 \quad\text{and}\quad ab = 0 \ \text{ or }\ ba = 0 \ \text{ for some } b \in R \text{ with } b \ne 0 .$$

The ring $R$ **has no zero divisors** when no element of $R$ is a zero divisor;
equivalently, when $ab = 0$ implies $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, for all $a, b \in R$.

An **integral domain**, or simply a **domain**, is a commutative ring
([[def-commutative-ring]]) $R$ such that

- **(D1)** $1 \ne 0$ in $R$;
- **(D2)** $R$ has no zero divisors.

In a commutative ring the two clauses $ab = 0$ and $ba = 0$ of the definition of
a zero divisor say the same thing, so there the notion is one-sided without
ambiguity.

**Two conventions fixed here, and kept.** First, $0$ is **not** a zero divisor,
because the clause $a \ne 0$ is part of the definition. This matters: $0 \cdot b = 0$
holds for every $b$ in every ring ([[lem-ring-elementary-consequences]]), so
without that clause $0$ would be a zero divisor in every ring with more than one
element and the phrase "no zero divisors" would name the empty class. Second,
(D1) is a **hypothesis and not a consequence** of (D2). The one-element ring, in
which $1 = 0$, has no zero divisors at all — vacuously, since it has no nonzero
element — so (D2) alone would admit it. It is excluded by (D1), and by nothing
else; the companion page records that ring explicitly.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map
$$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$
is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

derivations.claim: Define $c_0(f)$ to be the coefficient of $h^0$. By [F1], $c_0(fg)=c_0(f)c_0(g)$, while coefficientwise addition preserves sums; the constant-series map $k\to R$ is a right inverse, so $c_0$ is a surjective ring homomorphism. If $c_0(f)=0$, define $g_n=f_{n+1}$; then $f=hg$, so $\ker c_0\subseteq hR$. Conversely every multiple of $h$ has zero constant coefficient by the product formula. Hence $\ker c_0=hR$, and the induced map $R/hR\to k$ is a bijective ring homomorphism.

If $f,g\in R$ are nonzero, let $r$ and $s$ be their least indices with nonzero coefficients. In the convolution for the coefficient of $h^{r+s}$ in $fg$, every summand except the pair $(r,s)$ vanishes: a nonzero summand would require $i\ge r$, $j\ge s$, and $i+j=r+s$. The remaining coefficient is $f_rg_s\ne0$ by [F3]. Also $1_R\ne0_R$ because their constant coefficients are $1_k$ and $0_k$. Thus [F2] and [F4] show that $R$ is an integral domain.

A series lies in $h^nR$ exactly when its coefficients of degrees $0,\ldots,n-1$ vanish: one direction follows from multiplication by $h^n$, and the converse follows by shifting coefficients down by $n$. Therefore an $h$-adically Cauchy sequence $(f_j)$ has, for each $r\ge0$, an eventually constant coefficient of $h^r$; define $f_r$ to be that unique eventual value and let $f=\sum_{r\ge0}f_rh^r$. For any $n$, the Cauchy condition makes the first $n$ coefficients of $f_j$ agree with those of $f$ for all sufficiently large $j$, so $f_j-f\in h^nR$ eventually. This proves completeness. If $f\in\bigcap_{n\ge0}h^nR$, every coefficient of $f$ vanishes, so $f=0$; this proves separatedness. Applying the same construction to each of the finitely many standard coordinates of [F6] proves the assertion for every finite free $R$-module.
By step 1.2, $R$ is an integral domain, so [F5] applies: $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is a field and the canonical map $R\to K$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Every nonzero power series has a least degree with nonzero coefficient. By [F3], the coefficient of the least-degree term in a product of two nonzero series is the product of their two leading coefficients, which is nonzero by [F1]; hence [F4] confirms that $R$ is a domain. The module $M\subseteq R^n$ is therefore torsion-free: if $c\ne0$ and $cm=0$, every coordinate of $m$ is zero. The elements $p(e_1),\dots,p(e_n)$ from the standard basis of [F2] generate $M$, so $M/hM$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $k\cong R/hR$ by [F4].

Choose a basis $\bar m_1,\dots,\bar m_r$ of $M/hM$ and lifts $m_i\in M$. Let $N:=\sum_{i=1}^r Rm_i$ and $Q:=M/N$. The quotient $Q$ is finitely generated, and the spanning property modulo $h$ gives $M=N+hM$, hence $Q=hQ$.

Choose finite generators $q_1,\dots,q_s$ of $Q$. From $Q=hQ$, write $q_i=h\sum_{j=1}^s c_{ij}q_j$ with $c_{ij}\in R$. For the column $q=(q_i)$ this is $(I-hC)q=0$. The matrix series $\sum_{t\ge0}(hC)^t$ converges entrywise by [F4] and is a two-sided inverse of $I-hC$, since the finite partial products leave remainder $(hC)^{t+1}\in h^{t+1}M_s(R)$, which tends to zero; separatedness in [F4] makes the limiting products exactly the identity. Therefore every $q_i=0$, so $Q=0$ and the lifts $m_i$ span $M$. This also proves $M=0$ when $r=0$.

If $\sum_i a_im_i=0$ for $a_i\in R$, reducing modulo $h$ and using that the $\bar m_i$ are a basis gives $a_i\in hR$ for every $i$. Write $a_i=hb_i$ and cancel $h$ in $R^n$, which is torsion-free by step 1.1, to get $\sum_i b_im_i=0$. Repeating shows each $a_i\in h^tR$ for every $t\ge1$. A nonzero power series has a finite least degree, so $\bigcap_{t\ge1}h^tR=0$ by separatedness [F4], and every $a_i=0$. Thus the spanning family is linearly independent.

Steps 3.1 and 4.1 show that $(m_1,\dots,m_r)$ spans $M$ and is linearly independent, hence is an $R$-basis in the sense of [F2]. Its cardinality is $r=\dim_k(M/hM)$ by construction, proving the statement, including the empty basis when $r=0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

derivations.claim: By [F2], a finite $R$-basis identifies $A$ with $R^n$, so [F1] makes $A$ complete and separated. Multiplication is continuous: when $x'-x,y'-y\in h^rA$, expansion gives $x'y'-xy=(x'-x)y+x(y'-y)+(x'-x)(y'-y)\in h^rA$. For any idempotent $q$, the map $x\mapsto qxq$ is continuous and idempotent; its image is the kernel of the continuous map $1-(x\mapsto qxq)$, hence is closed in the separated module $A$ and is therefore complete.

In any such complete algebra $B$ with identity $q$, start with $a\in B$ satisfying $\delta:=a^2-a\in hB$. The element $u:=2a-q$ commutes with $\delta$ and satisfies $u^2=q+4\delta$. The partial sums $S_N:=\sum_{r=0}^N(-4\delta)^r$ are Cauchy because $\delta^r\in h^rB$; let $S$ be their limit. The finite geometric identity $(q+4\delta)S_N=q-(-4\delta)^{N+1}=S_N(q+4\delta)$ and separatedness give $(q+4\delta)S=S(q+4\delta)=q$, so $u^{-1}=uS=Su$. Set $a':=a-u^{-1}\delta$. The terms commute, and expansion gives $(a')^2-a'=\delta-u(u^{-1}\delta)+(u^{-1}\delta)^2=(u^{-1}\delta)^2$. Thus one correction squares the error and leaves the reduction of $a$ unchanged.

Starting with any lift $a_0$ of an idempotent in $B/hB$, apply step 2.1 repeatedly. If $a_n^2-a_n\in h^{r_n}B$, then $a_{n+1}-a_n\in h^{r_n}B$ and $a_{n+1}^2-a_{n+1}\in h^{2r_n}B$. Starting with $r_0=1$, we have $r_n=2^n$, so the sequence is Cauchy. Its limit $e$ exists by step 1.1; continuity of multiplication and the error tending to zero give $e^2=e$, and every correction lies in $hB$, so $e$ has the prescribed reduction.

Lift a complete orthogonal family by induction on $m$. If $m=0$, completeness means $1=0$ in $A/hA$; since $A$ is free of finite rank and $R/hR\cong k$ is a field, its reduction is $k^n$, so $A/hA=0$ forces its rank $n$ to be zero and hence $A=0$. The empty family then lifts. For $m=1$, the only member is $1$, which already lifts the family. For $m\ge2$, lift $\bar e_1$ by step 3.1 to an idempotent $e_1$ and set $q:=1-e_1$. The remaining reductions lie in the corner $\bar q(A/hA)\bar q$ and form a complete orthogonal family there. The reduction map $qAq\to\bar q(A/hA)\bar q$ is onto because any lift $x$ of a corner element can be replaced by $qxq$. Its kernel is $h(qAq)$: if $y\in qAq$ lies in $hA$, write $y=ha$; then $y=qyq=hqaq$ since $h$ is central by [F3], and the reverse inclusion is immediate. Thus the reduction identifies $qAq/h(qAq)$ with the indicated corner. The corner is complete by step 1.1, so induction lifts the remaining family in $qAq$; its members are orthogonal to $e_1$ since $qe_1=e_1q=0$, and their sum is $q$. This proves the claim for $m$.

The construction makes only finitely many initial lift choices, one for each member of the input finite family, and then applies the deterministic Newton recurrence in step 2.1. It uses no maximality principle or arbitrary family of choices. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 produce the required exact idempotents and preserve every prescribed reduction.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $S$ be a finite Coxeter generator set, and assume that the presented Coxeter group $W$ is finite. Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of odd-edge connected classes of $S$ from [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]: one class joins generators connected by a chain of finite odd braid labels. Introduce one invertible parameter $v_C$ for each $C\in\mathcal C$ and put $R_k:=k[v_C^{\pm1}:C\in\mathcal C]$. Let $H_{R_k}(W)$ be the scalar extension of the universal Hecke algebra to $R_k$; its relations are $(T_s-v_{[s]})(T_s+v_{[s]}^{-1})=0$ and the Coxeter braid relations. By [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], $H_{R_k}(W)$ is a free $R_k$-module with basis $(T_w)_{w\in W}$.

For a homomorphism of commutative rings $\phi:R_k\to K$ to a field $K$, define the specialized algebra $H_\phi:=K\otimes_{R_k}H_{R_k}(W)$ and use the same symbol $T_w$ for the specialized basis element $1\otimes T_w$. For $z\in H_\phi$, let $L_z:H_\phi\to H_\phi$ be left multiplication, $L_z(x)=zx$. The **regular-trace pairing** on $H_\phi$ is

$$B_\phi(x,y):=\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{xy}).$$

Its Gram matrix in the standard basis is $G_\phi=(\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{T_xT_y}))_{x,y\in W}$, and its **regular-trace determinant** is $D_\phi:=\det(G_\phi)$. The same construction over $R_k$ gives a Laurent polynomial $D_W\in R_k$.

Let $k$ be a field.

1. Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ a free $R$-module of finite rank $n$ with basis $(e_0,\dots,e_{n-1})$, and let $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in M$ span $M$. Then the coordinate matrix $A$ of $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ in the basis $(e_i)$ has a right inverse, $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$, and $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ is a basis of $M$. The determinant is formed for $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ the module is the zero module and the empty family is its basis, with no determinant clause.
2. If $F\subseteq E$ is a field extension and $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, then the rank of $A$ over $F$ equals its rank over $E$.
3. Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra and $N$ a finite-dimensional left $B$-module. A proper submodule has strictly smaller $k$-dimension, a maximal proper submodule of a nonzero finite-dimensional module exists by maximal dimension (no arbitrary Choice), and iterating produces a finite composition series of $N$ ([[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]); in particular $N$ has finite length.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $H$ is finite-dimensional and $B$ is its regular-trace pairing. Define $J:=\bigcap_S\operatorname{Ann}_H(S)$, intersecting over all simple left $H$-modules as in [F6]. This equals the intersection of all maximal left ideals: if $a$ lies in every maximal left ideal and $s\ne0$ lies in a simple module $S$, the map $H\to S$, $x\mapsto xs$, is onto and its kernel is maximal, so $as=0$; conversely, if $a$ annihilates every simple module then it kills $1+M$ in each simple quotient $H/M$, so $a\in M$ for every maximal left ideal $M$. In particular $J$ is a two-sided ideal.

By [F2], choose a finite composition series $0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=H$ of the left regular module. Since $J$ annihilates each simple factor $M_i/M_{i-1}$, $JM_i\subseteq M_{i-1}$ for every $i$. Repeating this inclusion gives $J^rH=0$, and then $J^r=0$ because $1\in H$.

Starting with $K_0=H$, if $K_i\ne J$ choose $x_i\in K_i\setminus J$. The equality in step 1.1 gives a maximal left ideal $N_i$ not containing $x_i$; then $K_{i+1}:=K_i\cap N_i$ strictly contains $J$ and has strictly smaller $K$-dimension than $K_i$. Thus after at most $\dim_K H$ steps the intersection is $J$. This finite descent selects finitely many maximal left ideals and uses no arbitrary Choice.

For $j\in J$ and $b\in H$, the two-sided-ideal property gives $jb\in J$; by step 1.2, $(jb)^r=0$. Hence $L_{jb}^r=L_{(jb)^r}=0$, so [F4] gives $B(j,b)=\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{jb})=0$ for every $b\in H$.

The map $H/J\to\bigoplus_i H/N_i$ sending $x+J$ to $(x+N_i)_i$ is an injective $H$-module homomorphism: its kernel is $(\bigcap_iN_i)/J=0$, and each quotient $H/N_i$ is simple by [F6]. By [F3] its image is semisimple, so $H/J$ is semisimple.
Nondegeneracy of $B$ and step 2.2 imply $j=0$ for every $j\in J$, hence $J=0$. Therefore $H\cong H/J$ is semisimple by step 3.1 and [F5]. No separable-division-algebra trace converse is used.

citations.quote: Let $k$ be a field, $R:=k\llbracket h\rrbracket$ the ring of formal power series with its $h$-adic topology, and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free of finite rank. An **idempotent** is an element $e$ with $e^2=e$; idempotents $e_i$ are **orthogonal** if $e_ie_j=0$ whenever $i\ne j$, and a finite orthogonal family is **complete** if its sum is $1$. Every finite complete orthogonal family $(\bar e_1,\dots,\bar e_m)$ in $A/hA$ has a lift to a finite complete orthogonal family $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ in $A$, with $e_i+hA=\bar e_i$ for each $i$.

Let $k$ be a field and $R:=k\llbracket h\rrbracket$. For $n\ge0$, let $p:R^n\to R^n$ be an $R$-linear map with $p^2=p$, and put $M:=p(R^n)$. Then $M$ is free of finite rank equal to $r:=\dim_k(M/hM)$. This includes $M=0$ and $r=0$.

Let $k$ be a field and $R:=k\llbracket h\rrbracket$, with formal series understood as coefficient functions and multiplication given by finite Cauchy convolution. The constant-coefficient map $c_0:R\to k$ is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $hR$, so it induces $R/hR\cong k$. The ring $R$ is an integral domain. For the $h$-adic topology, whose neighborhoods of zero are $h^nR$ for $n\ge0$, $R$ is complete and separated; every finite free module $R^m$ is complete and separated coefficientwise. Finally, $K:=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is a field, and the canonical map $R\to K$ is injective.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\in R\llbracket x\rrbracket$. Then $f$ is a unit in $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ if and only if $a_0$ is a unit in $R$.

When $a_0$ is a unit, the inverse $g=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n$ is unique and is determined by

$$b_0=a_0^{-1},\qquad b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_{n-i}\quad(n\ge1).$$

The criterion also holds in the zero ring.

derivations.claim: If $\Lambda$ is empty, then $A/hA=0$; since a finite free module of rank $n$ reduces to $k^n$ and $k\ne0$ by [F3, F4], this forces $n=0$ and hence $A=0$, so the empty product conclusion holds. Otherwise, for each standard diagonal matrix idempotent $\bar e_{\lambda,a}$ in the given reduction choose the finite complete orthogonal family of all such idempotents. By [F1] it lifts to pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_{\lambda,a}\in A$ whose sum is $1$.

For any two lifted diagonal idempotents $e_i,e_j$, the map $p_{ij}:A\to A$, $x\mapsto e_i x e_j$, is an idempotent $R$-linear projection with image $e_iAe_j$. The decomposition $A=\operatorname{im}(p_{ij})\oplus\ker(p_{ij})$ reduces modulo $h$ to the corresponding image/kernel decomposition of $\bar p_{ij}$; hence $(e_iAe_j)/h(e_iAe_j)\cong\bar e_i(A/hA)\bar e_j$. In the specified product of matrix algebras this corner has dimension $1$ when $i,j$ belong to the same block and dimension $0$ when they belong to different blocks. Applying [F2] after identifying the finite free module $A$ with $R^n$ shows that same-block corners are free of rank $1$ and cross-block corners are zero.

Fix one block $\lambda$ and its first diagonal idempotent $e_{\lambda,1}$. For each $a$ choose lifts $x_{\lambda,a}\in e_{\lambda,a}Ae_{\lambda,1}$ and $y_{\lambda,a}\in e_{\lambda,1}Ae_{\lambda,a}$ of the standard matrix units $E_{a1}$ and $E_{1a}$. Each corner is free of rank $1$ by step 2.1; an element whose reduction is nonzero is a basis, because its coefficient relative to any basis has nonzero constant term and is therefore a unit by [F5]. Thus $y_{\lambda,a}x_{\lambda,a}=c_a e_{\lambda,1}$ with $c_a\equiv1\pmod h$; replacing $y_{\lambda,a}$ by $c_a^{-1}y_{\lambda,a}$ gives $y_{\lambda,a}x_{\lambda,a}=e_{\lambda,1}$. Also $x_{\lambda,a}y_{\lambda,a}=d_a e_{\lambda,a}$ with $d_a\equiv1\pmod h$. This product is idempotent because $y_{\lambda,a}x_{\lambda,a}=e_{\lambda,1}$, so $d_a^2=d_a$; since $d_a\equiv1\pmod h$ is a unit by [F5], $d_a=1$. Hence $x_{\lambda,a}y_{\lambda,a}=e_{\lambda,a}$.

Define $E_{\lambda,ab}:=x_{\lambda,a}y_{\lambda,b}$. If $b=c$ then $y_{\lambda,b}x_{\lambda,c}=e_{\lambda,1}$, and if $b\ne c$ then this product is zero by orthogonality of $e_{\lambda,b},e_{\lambda,c}$. Therefore $E_{\lambda,ab}E_{\lambda,cd}=\delta_{bc}E_{\lambda,ad}$. Products between distinct blocks vanish by the zero cross-block corners of step 2.1, and $\sum_{\lambda,a}E_{\lambda,aa}=\sum_{\lambda,a}e_{\lambda,a}=1$. Their reductions are exactly all standard matrix units.

The total number of elements $E_{\lambda,ab}$ is $\dim_k(A/hA)=\operatorname{rank}_R(A)$ by [F3, F4]. Relative to an $R$-basis of $A$, their coordinate matrix $C$ reduces to an invertible matrix $C_0$ over $k$, so $C=C_0+hC_1$ for some matrix $C_1$. The factorization $C=C_0(I+hC_0^{-1}C_1)$ is invertible: the partial sums of $\sum_{m\ge0}(-hC_0^{-1}C_1)^m$ converge entrywise by completeness in [F3], and the finite geometric identity plus separatedness in [F3] makes the limit the two-sided inverse of the second factor. Thus the lifted matrix units form an $R$-basis by [F4]. The linear map from the product of matrix algebras sending standard matrix units to $E_{\lambda,ab}$ is multiplicative by step 4.1, is unital, and maps a basis to a basis; it is the claimed algebra isomorphism.

Let $S$ be a finite set and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ satisfy $m(s,s)=1$ for all $s\in S$ and $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ for all $s\ne t$. Such an $m$ is a **Coxeter matrix** on $S$.

**The presented group.** Let $R\subseteq F(S)$ be the set of relators
$$R:=\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s,t\in S,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},$$
where $F(S)$ is the free group on $S$ ([[def-free-group]], [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]) and $(st)^k$ is the $k$-fold product ([[def-group-power]]), and let $N:=\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(S)}$ be the normal closure of $R$ in $F(S)$ ([[def-normal-closure]], [[prop-normal-closure-is-products-of-conjugates]]). Define
$$W:=F(S)/N,$$
and write $s$ (as well as $sN$) for the image of $s\in S$ in $W$ ([[def-quotient-group]], [[def-group]]).

**Universal property.** For every group $G$ and every map $f:S\to G$ with $f(s)^2=1$ for all $s\in S$ and $(f(s)f(t))^{m(s,t)}=1$ in $G$ for all $s\ne t$ with $m(s,t)<\infty$, there is a unique group homomorphism $\varphi:W\to G$ with $\varphi(s)=f(s)$ for all $s\in S$ ([[def-group-homomorphism]], [[thm-quotient-group-universal-property]], [[thm-von-dyck]], [[def-group-presentation]], [[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]], [[prop-equality-of-words-in-a-presentation]]).

**Length and reduced words.** For $w\in W$ put
$$\ell(w):=\min\{k\in\mathbb{N}:\ \text{there exist }s_1,\dots,s_k\in S\text{ with }w=s_1\cdots s_k\}.$$
The minimum exists: every element of the free group $F(S)$ is represented by a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ ([[def-alphabet-words-and-reduction]]), and $s^{-1}=s$ in $W$ because $s^2\in R$, so every element of $W$ is the value of a finite word in $S$; the set of admissible $k\in\mathbb{N}$ is therefore nonempty and has a least element by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]], [[def-natural-numbers]]). A word $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ in $S$ is a **reduced expression** of $w$ when $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and $k=\ell(w)$, and **nonreduced** otherwise. The empty word $(\;)$ is a word in $S$ of length $0$, and $\ell(1)=0$; it is the reduced expression of $1$.

**Terminology.** The pair $(W,S)$ is the **Coxeter system** presented by the Coxeter matrix $(S,m)$; when $s\mapsto s$ is understood, we also say that $W$ is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

**Standard parabolic subgroups.** For $J\subseteq S$ put $W_J:=\langle\{s:s\in J\}\rangle\le W$ ([[def-generated-subgroup]]).

**Conventions.** $m(s,t)$ is declared to be the order of $st$ in $W$; a value $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relator on $s,t$. This definition asserts no finiteness, faithfulness, or completeness property of the presentation: the statements that the elements $s\in S$ are pairwise distinct in $W$ (so that $S$ may be viewed as a labelled subset of $W$), that $\ell(s)=1$, that a word is reduced exactly when it admits no two-letter deletion, and that $(W_J,J)$ is the Coxeter system presented by the restricted matrix $m|_J$ with intrinsic length equal to the ambient length are recorded with their justifiers below and are not used before those results.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group and $\ell$ its length function ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Write $s\sim t$ when there exist $s=s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k=t$ in $S$ with $m(s_i,s_{i+1})$ odd for every $i<k$; this is the connected-component relation of the graph on $S$ whose edges are the pairs with odd $m$, and it is an equivalence relation (1.1). Let $[s]$ denote the class of $s$ and let $c$ be the number of classes.

**Coefficient ring.** Put $R:=\mathbb Z[v_1^{\pm1},\dots,v_c^{\pm1}]=\Lambda_{\mathbb Z,c}$, the Laurent polynomial ring in $c$ variables ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2): a commutative ring in which every $v_i$ is a unit. Identify the classes with $\{1,\dots,c\}$ and put $v_s:=v_{[s]}\in R^\times$ for $s\in S$.

**The generic Hecke algebra.** Let $F:=R\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $R$-algebra on $S$ and let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], part 2) by the **quadratic relations**
$$(T_s-v_s)(T_s+v_s^{-1})\qquad(s\in S)$$
and the **braid relations**
$$T_sT_tT_s\cdots=T_tT_sT_t\cdots\qquad(s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty),$$
both alternating products having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $H:=H(W):=F/I$ and write $T_s$ for the image of the generator $T_s$. Then $H$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) with the following **universal property**: for every unital associative $R$-algebra $A$ and every family $(t_s)_{s\in S}$ in $A$ satisfying the same two families of relations, there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $H\to A$ with $T_s\mapsto t_s$.

**Universal parameters.** For every commutative ring $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_c\in A^\times$ the assignment $v_i\mapsto u_i$ extends uniquely to a ring homomorphism $R\to A$ ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2); via the universal property of $H$ this makes $R$ the universal coefficient ring for a unit-valued parameter that is constant on each class $[s]$.

**Generator conjugacy.** Two simple generators $s,t\in S$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $s\sim t$.

**Conventions and scope.** (i) $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$; if $c=1$ we write $v$ for $v_1$. (ii) The quadratic relation is equivalent to $T_s^2-(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$, equivalently $(T_s+v_s^{-1})(T_s-v_s)=0$, and it depends on $v_s$ only through the difference $v_s-v_s^{-1}$ (1.6). (iii) No freeness, torsion-freeness, specialisation or basis property of $H$ is asserted here: the elements $T_w$ are introduced in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]], their independence is proved in [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and the invertibility and bar properties are recorded in [[lem-hh-hecke-anti-involution-bar-and-normalization]]; consumers may not use those features before those items.

Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $X$ be a set and let $R\langle X\rangle$ be the free $R$-algebra on $X$ ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]).

1. There is a unique $S$-algebra isomorphism $S\otimes_RR\langle X\rangle\to S\langle X\rangle$ with $s\otimes x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}\mapsto s\,x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}$ on words; its inverse sends a word to $1\otimes$ that word.
2. If $I\subseteq R\langle X\rangle$ is a two-sided ideal, then there is a unique $S$-algebra isomorphism $S\otimes_R\bigl(R\langle X\rangle/I\bigr)\cong(S\otimes_RR\langle X\rangle)/\operatorname{im}(S\otimes_RI)$, sending $s\otimes(y+I)$ to $(s\otimes y)+\operatorname{im}(S\otimes_RI)$, the image ideal being generated by the images of the relations. No flatness or freeness of $S$ over $R$ is assumed.
3. If an $R$-algebra $A$ is free as an $R$-module with basis $(a_i)$, then $S\otimes_RA$ is a free $S$-module with basis $(1\otimes a_i)$. Consequently an explicitly constructed basis isomorphism of a presentation may be tensored with $S$ to give a basis in every commutative specialization.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $R$, $v_s$, $H$, $T_s$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]; let $T_w$ for $w\in W$ and the spanning statement be as in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]]; and let $E$, $P_s$, $Q_s$ and $P_w$ be as in [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

1. **The length-operator representation.** There is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(E)$ with $\rho(T_s)=P_s$ for all $s\in S$; it satisfies $\rho(T_w)=P_w$ and $\rho(T_w)(e_1)=e_w$ for all $w\in W$.
2. **Standard basis.** $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$: it spans by [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]] and is $R$-linearly independent. Hence $H$ is free as an $R$-module and every element of $H$ has a unique expansion $\sum_wa_wT_w$ with $a_w\in R$ and all but finitely many $a_w$ zero.
3. **Faithfulness.** $\rho$ is injective.
4. **Base change.** For every commutative ring $R'$ and every ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to R'$, the scalar extension $R'\otimes_RH$ is, as an $R'$-algebra, canonically isomorphic to the quotient of the free associative $R'$-algebra on $(T_s)_{s\in S}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the images under $\varphi$ of the relations (Q) and (B) of [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], and it is free as an $R'$-module with basis $(1\otimes T_w)_{w\in W}$. No flatness or freeness of $R'$ over $R$ is assumed, and no torsion-freeness or semisimplicity of $H$ or of its specialisations is claimed.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $n\ge0$.

1. **Multivariate polynomial ring.** The ring $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] is a commutative $R$-algebra, free as an $R$-module on the monomials $x^\alpha=x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}$ ($\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$), and for every commutative $R$-algebra $A$ and elements $a_1,\dots,a_n\in A$ there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to A$ with $x_i\mapsto a_i$. If $R$ is an integral domain, so is $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.
2. **Laurent polynomial ring.** The set $\Lambda_{R,n}$ of finitely supported functions $\mathbb Z^n\to R$ with coefficientwise addition and convolution $(ab)_\gamma=\sum_{\alpha+\beta=\gamma}a_\alpha b_\beta$ (summed only over the finite supports of $a$ and $b$) is a commutative $R$-algebra, free as an $R$-module on the monomials $x^\alpha$ ($\alpha\in\mathbb Z^n$); each $x_i$ is a unit. For every commutative $R$-algebra $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_n\in A$ there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $\Lambda_{R,n}\to A$ with $x_i\mapsto u_i$. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $S$ be a finite Coxeter generator set, and assume that the presented Coxeter group $W$ is finite. Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of odd-edge connected classes of $S$ from [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]: one class joins generators connected by a chain of finite odd braid labels. Introduce one invertible parameter $v_C$ for each $C\in\mathcal C$ and put $R_k:=k[v_C^{\pm1}:C\in\mathcal C]$. $$B_\phi(x,y):=\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{xy}).$$

derivations.claim: Specialize every parameter $v_C$ to $1$ and call the resulting algebra $H_1$. By [F2], each specialized generator $T_s$ is an involution and the alternating braid relations hold. For involutions $a,b$, put $g:=ab$, so $ba=g^{-1}$. If $m=2r$, the braid relation is $g^r=g^{-r}$, equivalent to $g^{2r}=1$. If $m=2r+1$, its two sides are $g^ra$ and $(ba)^rb$; right multiplication by $a$ makes equality equivalent to $g^r=(ba)^{r+1}=g^{-(r+1)}$, which is equivalent to $g^{2r+1}=1$. Thus, for every finite braid label, braid and Coxeter relator are equivalent in the presence of the involution relations. The specialized generators satisfy exactly [F1].

If $\phi:R_k\to K$ is a field homomorphism with $\phi(D_W)\ne0$, [F7] says that the regular-trace Gram matrix of $H_\phi$ has nonzero determinant and is therefore nondegenerate. Applying [F6] shows that $H_\phi$ is semisimple. This criterion does not infer splitness and makes no claim when $\phi(D_W)=0$.

By the group universal property in [F1], $s\mapsto T_s$ extends to $W\to H_1^\times$, and linear extension gives a $k$-algebra map $kW\to H_1$. Conversely, the group generators in $kW$ satisfy the specialized quadratic and braid relations, so the quotient presentation in [F3] gives a $k$-algebra map $H_1\to kW$. The composites are identity on their algebra generators, hence $H_1\cong kW$ and $T_w$ corresponds to $w$. By [F4], $(T_w)_{w\in W}$ is a basis of $H_1$, so $\dim_kH_1=|W|$.

Thus $\operatorname{Tr}_k(L_g)=|W|$ for $g=1$ and $0$ otherwise. Since $k$ is a field, [F5] makes $R_k$ an integral domain and embeds it into its fraction field $F$; therefore $D_W$ remains nonzero in $F$. When $|W|=1$, the matrix in step 3.1 is $[1]$, so the argument includes the trivial Coxeter group. All bases are finite and specified; no form of Choice is used.

$$A\cong\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\operatorname{Mat}_{d_\lambda}(R)$$

Let $k$ be a field and $R:=k\llbracket h\rrbracket$, with formal series understood as coefficient functions and multiplication given by finite Cauchy convolution. The constant-coefficient map $c_0:R\to k$ is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $hR$, so it induces $R/hR\cong k$. The ring $R$ is an integral domain. A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are
$0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M\ne0$ and $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $A\cong\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\operatorname{Mat}_{d_\lambda}(R)$. Reducing this isomorphism modulo $h$ and using $R/hR\cong k$ from [F4] gives the stated product for the special fiber. Tensoring the matrix-unit basis with the field $K$ gives $K\otimes_R A\cong\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\operatorname{Mat}_{d_\lambda}(K)$. The lifted block identities $p_\lambda=\sum_{a=1}^{d_\lambda}E_{\lambda,aa}$ reduce to the specified block identities and extend to the generic fiber.

Let $L$ be any field and $d\ge1$. If $v\in L^d$ is nonzero, choose a nonzero coordinate $v_j$; for each $i$, the matrix unit $E_{ij}$ sends $v$ to $v_je_i$, and scalar multiplication by $v_j^{-1}$ produces $e_i$. Thus the natural left module $L^d$ is simple. Conversely, let $S$ be a simple left $\operatorname{Mat}_d(L)$-module. Since $1=\sum_iE_{ii}$ and $S\ne0$, choose $i$ and $s\in S$ with $E_{ii}s\ne0$. Define the $L$-linear map $L^d\to S$ by $e_j\mapsto E_{ji}s$. It intertwines the action of each matrix unit because $E_{pq}E_{ji}=\delta_{qj}E_{pi}$; since matrix units form an $L$-basis of the algebra, it is a module homomorphism. It is nonzero, so its image is all of $S$ by simplicity; its kernel is a submodule of the simple natural module and is not the whole module, so it is zero. Hence every simple module for one matrix factor is its natural module and is unique up to isomorphism.

In a finite product of matrix algebras, the central block identities are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$. On a nonzero simple module their images are submodules whose sum is direct and equals the module. At least one image is nonzero; if two were nonzero, each would be a proper nonzero submodule, contradicting simplicity. Therefore exactly one block identity has nonzero image, that identity acts as the identity, and all others act as zero. Step 1.2 classifies the simple module for the unique acting factor. The same lifted $p_\lambda$ labels the corresponding factors in the special and generic fibers, and each natural module has dimension $d_\lambda$.

For any finite Hecke specialization with $D_W\ne0$, [F3] says its regular-trace Gram determinant is nonzero, so its regular-trace pairing is nondegenerate; [F2] then gives semisimplicity. If $D_W=0$, [F2] gives no conclusion. This proves the stated scope of the exceptional parameter set and does not infer labels or splitness for these general fibers.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group and $\ell$ its length function ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Write $s\sim t$ when there exist $s=s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k=t$ in $S$ with $m(s_i,s_{i+1})$ odd for every $i<k$; this is the connected-component relation of the graph on $S$ whose edges are the pairs with odd $m$, and it is an equivalence relation (1.1). Let $[s]$ denote the class of $s$ and let $c$ be the number of classes.

**Coefficient ring.** Put $R:=\mathbb Z[v_1^{\pm1},\dots,v_c^{\pm1}]=\Lambda_{\mathbb Z,c}$, the Laurent polynomial ring in $c$ variables ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2): a commutative ring in which every $v_i$ is a unit. Identify the classes with $\{1,\dots,c\}$ and put $v_s:=v_{[s]}\in R^\times$ for $s\in S$.

**The generic Hecke algebra.** Let $F:=R\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $R$-algebra on $S$ and let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], part 2) by the **quadratic relations**
$$(T_s-v_s)(T_s+v_s^{-1})\qquad(s\in S)$$
and the **braid relations**
$$T_sT_tT_s\cdots=T_tT_sT_t\cdots\qquad(s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty),$$
both alternating products having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $H:=H(W):=F/I$ and write $T_s$ for the image of the generator $T_s$. Then $H$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) with the following **universal property**: for every unital associative $R$-algebra $A$ and every family $(t_s)_{s\in S}$ in $A$ satisfying the same two families of relations, there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $H\to A$ with $T_s\mapsto t_s$.

**Universal parameters.** For every commutative ring $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_c\in A^\times$ the assignment $v_i\mapsto u_i$ extends uniquely to a ring homomorphism $R\to A$ ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2); via the universal property of $H$ this makes $R$ the universal coefficient ring for a unit-valued parameter that is constant on each class $[s]$.

**Generator conjugacy.** Two simple generators $s,t\in S$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $s\sim t$.

**Conventions and scope.** (i) $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$; if $c=1$ we write $v$ for $v_1$. (ii) The quadratic relation is equivalent to $T_s^2-(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$, equivalently $(T_s+v_s^{-1})(T_s-v_s)=0$, and it depends on $v_s$ only through the difference $v_s-v_s^{-1}$ (1.6). derivations.claim: Since $i^{-1}=-i$, the defining polynomial is $(T-i)^2$, and the standard basis is $(1,T)$ by [F2]. Expanding the relation gives $T^2=1+2iT$.

Let $\epsilon:=T-i$. The basis $(1,T)$ implies $\epsilon\ne0$, while the defining polynomial gives $\epsilon^2=0$. For any simple left $H$-module $S$, $\epsilon S$ is a submodule because $H$ is commutative. If $\epsilon S\ne0$, simplicity [F4] gives $\epsilon S=S$, and applying $\epsilon$ again yields $0=\epsilon^2S=\epsilon S=S$, a contradiction. Thus $\epsilon$ annihilates every simple module.

In the basis $(1,T)$, the columns of $L_T$ are $(0,1)^{\mathsf T}$ and $(1,2i)^{\mathsf T}$, so $[L_T]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2i\end{pmatrix}$. Hence the regular-trace Gram matrix is $G=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Tr}(L_1)&\operatorname{Tr}(L_T)\\\operatorname{Tr}(L_T)&\operatorname{Tr}(L_{T^2})\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&2i\\2i&-2\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $-4-(2i)^2=0$, so the regular-trace pairing is degenerate and the regular-trace determinant vanishes.

Define $\tau(1)=1$ and $\tau(T)=0$. From $T^2=1+2iT$, for $x=a+bT$ and $y=c+dT$ one obtains $\tau(xy)=ac+bd=\tau(yx)$. Its Gram matrix in $(1,T)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so the pairing $\tau(xy)$ is nondegenerate and perfect.

If the regular module $H$ were semisimple, it would be a direct sum of simple submodules by [F5], each annihilated by $\epsilon$ by step 1.2; then $\epsilon$ would annihilate all of $H$. But $\epsilon\cdot1=\epsilon\ne0$. Therefore $H$ is not semisimple, despite the perfect symmetrizing pairing in step 2.2. This refutes the statement.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$.

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

For every commutative ring $R$, the coefficientwise addition and convolution multiplication of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]] make $R[x]$ a commutative ring. The constant-polynomial map $c\colon R\to R[x]$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **formal power series over $R$** is a coefficient function $a:\mathbb N\to R$, written

$$f=\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n,$$

and $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ is the set of all such functions. The symbol $x$ is an indeterminate. The notation asserts no analytic convergence and no value of $x$ is being chosen.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, the **coefficient-extraction functional** is evaluation at $n$:

$$[x^n]f:=a_n.$$

Define zero and one coefficientwise, put $[x^n](f+g)=[x^n]f+[x^n]g$, and define the Cauchy product by

$$[x^n](fg)=\sum_{i+j=n}[x^i]f\,[x^j]g=\sum_{i=0}^{n}[x^i]f\,[x^{n-i}]g.$$

The last sum is finite, including when $n=0$. The constant $r\in R$ denotes the series with coefficient $r$ at $0$ and $0$ elsewhere. The series $x$ has coefficient $1$ at $1$ and $0$ elsewhere. Thus $x^0=1$, and $x^n$ is supported at $n$.

The finitely supported coefficient functions form the polynomial part of $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$. Under the coefficient-function definition of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], a polynomial is therefore the same data as a finitely supported formal series; the next theorem verifies that this identification respects the ring operations.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\in R\llbracket x\rrbracket$. Then $f$ is a unit in $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ if and only if $a_0$ is a unit in $R$.

When $a_0$ is a unit, the inverse $g=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n$ is unique and is determined by

$$b_0=a_0^{-1},\qquad b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_{n-i}\quad(n\ge1).$$

The criterion also holds in the zero ring.

A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are
$0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M\ne0$ and $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

$(\mathbb{Q}, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ with the operations of [[def-rat-operations]]

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and

  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Fix $r,n\ge1$ and use the independent units $Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r$ of [[def-hh-multiplicative-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]]. An **$r$-multipartition** of $n$ is a tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(r)})$ of ordinary partitions whose total number of boxes is $n$. Its boxes are triples $(c,a,b)$ with $1\le c\le r$, $a\ge1$, and $1\le b\le\lambda^{(c)}_a$. Order the boxes within component $c$ by the transitive closure of $(c,a,b)<(c,a,b+1)$ and $(c,a,b)<(c,a+1,b)$; boxes in different components are incomparable.

A **standard multitableau** $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is a bijective filling of the boxes by $1,\ldots,n$ that increases along every row and column. Equivalently, it is a linear extension of this finite box poset. Write $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ for the set of such fillings and

$$ \operatorname{res}_t(i)=u_cQ^{b-a}\quad\text{if entry }i\text{ occupies }(c,a,b). $$

The **generic content field** is $K=\mathbb Q(Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r)$, the fraction field of $R$. The contents of distinct addable boxes of any multipartition are distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have the same content, they lie on one diagonal; the right and lower boxes immediately between them are distinct required predecessors of the southeast box. Consequently, for three consecutive labels $i,i+1,i+2$ in a standard multitableau, the first and third contents cannot agree. In particular every pair of contents among three consecutive labels is distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have content exponents differing by $1$, then they are comparable in the box order, so interchanging adjacent labels in a standard multitableau never gives a content ratio $Q$ or $Q^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: The dominance inequalities are reflexive and transitive. If they hold in both directions, all displayed cumulative sums are equal; subtracting successive row cutoffs and then successive component prefixes recovers every row length in every component, so $\lambda=\mu$. Thus $\unrhd$ is a partial order. The tableau $t^\lambda$ is standard: its entries increase left to right by construction, and every box in an earlier row or earlier component is filled before every box in a later row or component, so each column also increases top to bottom.

Fix $\lambda$. If $\mu>\lambda$, the cell axiom applied to $C^\mu_{u,v}a$ puts it in the span of the shape-$\mu$ basis elements plus $A^{>\mu}$. Every shape in that expression is strictly above $\lambda$ by transitivity; hence $A^{>\lambda}$ is a right ideal. Since $*$ preserves each shape and $A^{>\lambda}$, $a x=(x^*a^*)^*$ lies in $A^{>\lambda}$ whenever $x$ does, so it is also a left ideal. The same argument with $\mu\ge\lambda$ proves that $A^{\ge\lambda}$ is a two-sided ideal.

The given basis of $A^{\ge\lambda}$ is the disjoint union of the shape-$\lambda$ basis and the basis of $A^{>\lambda}$. Linear independence therefore makes the classes of $C^\lambda_{s,t}$ a basis of the quotient $A^{\ge\lambda}/A^{>\lambda}$. No choice is needed because the poset and every indexing set are finite.

Fix integers $r,n\ge1$. Put $R=\mathbb Z[Q^{\pm1},u_1^{\pm1},\ldots,u_r^{\pm1}]$ and $p(X)=\prod_{a=1}^r(X-u_a)$. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ be the unital associative $R$-algebra on generators $T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ and $X_1^{\pm1},\ldots,X_n^{\pm1}$, with central $R$-action, subject to

$$ (T_i-Q)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\ (|i-j|>1), $$

$$ X_jX_k=X_kX_j,\qquad T_iX_j=X_jT_i\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad T_iX_iT_i=QX_{i+1}. $$

Here the braid relation is imposed for $1\le i<n-1$ and the distant commutation relation for $1\le i,j<n$. Define the **multiplicative cyclotomic Hecke algebra of level $r$ and rank $n$** by

$$ H_{r,n}=\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{aff}}/(p(X_1)), $$

where $(p(X_1))$ denotes the two-sided ideal it generates. The unit $Q$ and the quadratic relation make every $T_i$ invertible, with $T_i^{-1}=Q^{-1}(T_i-(Q-1))$. The cyclotomic relation also gives the polynomial inverse

$$ X_1^{-1}=(-1)^{r+1}(u_1\cdots u_r)^{-1}\bigl(X_1^{r-1}-e_1X_1^{r-2}+\cdots+(-1)^{r-1}e_{r-1}\bigr), $$

where $e_k$ is the $k$th elementary symmetric polynomial in $u_1,\ldots,u_r$. The presentation already includes inverse generators; this formula records that the quotient does not require a separate inverse parameter. For $i\ge1$, write $X_{i+1}=Q^{-1}T_iX_iT_i$ when using the recursion determined by the affine relation.

This is the multiplicative presentation. It is not the additive degenerate cyclotomic presentation obtained after setting a parameter equal to $1$ and changing generators.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S$ a set. There is a unital associative $R$-algebra $R\langle S\rangle$, the **free associative $R$-algebra on $S$**, whose underlying $R$-module is free on the set of finite words in $S$ (including the empty word), with product given on words by concatenation and extended $R$-bilinearly.

1. **Universal property.** For every $R$-algebra $A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every map $S\to A$ there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $R\langle S\rangle\to A$ extending it. When $R=k$ is a field and $S$ indexes a basis of a vector space $V$, $R\langle S\rangle$ reproduces the published tensor algebra $T(V)$ ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]).
2. **Two-sided ideal description.** For $E\subseteq R\langle S\rangle$ the two-sided ideal $(E)$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in R\langle S\rangle$ and $e_s\in E$.
3. **Quotient universal property.** If $\varphi:R\langle S\rangle\to A$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism killing $E$, then $\varphi$ factors uniquely through the quotient $R\langle S\rangle/(E)$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]); the quotient is the presented $R$-algebra with generators $S$ and relations $E$.

In $H_{r,n}$ define

$$ L_1=X_1,\qquad L_i=Q^{1-i}T_{i-1}\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_{i-1}\quad(2\le i\le n). $$

Then $L_i=X_i$ for every $i$, so the $L_i$ commute and are units. For $1\le i<n$ they satisfy

$$ T_iL_iT_i=QL_{i+1},\qquad T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(Q-1)L_{i+1},\qquad T_iL_{i+1}=L_iT_i+(Q-1)L_{i+1}, $$

and $T_iL_j=L_jT_i$ when $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$. More generally, for every polynomial $f\in R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$,

$$ T_if(L_1,\ldots,L_n)=f(s_iL_1,\ldots,s_iL_n)T_i-(Q-1)L_{i+1}\frac{f(L_1,\ldots,L_n)-f(s_iL_1,\ldots,s_iL_n)}{L_i-L_{i+1}}, $$

where $s_i$ interchanges the $i$th and $(i+1)$st variables and the displayed divided difference is a polynomial. In particular the cyclotomic relation transports as

$$ T_ip(L_i)=p(L_{i+1})T_i-(Q-1)L_{i+1}\frac{p(L_i)-p(L_{i+1})}{L_i-L_{i+1}}. $$

When $p(L_i)=0$, this gives $p(L_{i+1})T_i=(Q-1)L_{i+1}(p(L_i)-p(L_{i+1}))/(L_i-L_{i+1})$; the cyclotomic quotient guarantees this only for $i=1$. It does **not** impose $p(L_i)=0$ for every $i$.

derivations.claim: On the free associative algebra define $*$ by $r^*=r$ for $r\in R$, $T_i^*=T_i$, $X_j^*=X_j$, $(X_j^{-1})^*=X_j^{-1}$, and $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$, extending $R$-linearly. Word reversal is an involutive anti-automorphism, so this defines an involutive anti-automorphism of the free algebra.

The quadratic relation is a polynomial in one fixed generator and is fixed by reversal. Each braid word in the $T_i$ is palindromic, each distant commutation relation reverses to the same equality with sides exchanged, each relation $X_jX_k=X_kX_j$ and $T_iX_j=X_jT_i$ reverses to its equivalent reversed equality, and $T_iX_iT_i=QX_{i+1}$ is fixed because its left word is palindromic and $Q$ is central. The inverse relations reverse to the other inverse equations, and the cyclotomic relation $p(X_1)=0$ is fixed because it is a polynomial in $X_1$. Thus reversal sends every defining relator into the defining ideal. As the ideal is two-sided, it is preserved under reversal, so $*$ descends to an involutive anti-automorphism of $H_{r,n}$.

The quotient is generated by the displayed letters and $R$, so any anti-homomorphism fixing them is unique. By [F3], $L_j=X_j$, hence $L_j^*=L_j$. On words in the finite generators $T_i$, reversal sends a reduced word for $w$ to the reversed reduced word for $w^{-1}$; therefore $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, as for the finite reversal anti-involution.

$$ T_if(L_1,\ldots,L_n)=f(s_iL_1,\ldots,s_iL_n)T_i-(Q-1)L_{i+1}\frac{f(L_1,\ldots,L_n)-f(s_iL_1,\ldots,s_iL_n)}{L_i-L_{i+1}}, $$

$$ T_ip(L_i)=p(L_{i+1})T_i-(Q-1)L_{i+1}\frac{p(L_i)-p(L_{i+1})}{L_i-L_{i+1}}. $$

When $p(L_i)=0$, this gives $p(L_{i+1})T_i=(Q-1)L_{i+1}(p(L_i)-p(L_{i+1}))/(L_i-L_{i+1})$; the cyclotomic quotient guarantees this only for $i=1$. It does **not** impose $p(L_i)=0$ for every $i$.

Fix integers $r,n\ge1$. Put $R=\mathbb Z[Q^{\pm1},u_1^{\pm1},\ldots,u_r^{\pm1}]$ and $p(X)=\prod_{a=1}^r(X-u_a)$. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ be the unital associative $R$-algebra on generators $T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ and $X_1^{\pm1},\ldots,X_n^{\pm1}$, with central $R$-action, subject to

$$ (T_i-Q)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\ (|i-j|>1), $$

$$ X_jX_k=X_kX_j,\qquad T_iX_j=X_jT_i\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad T_iX_iT_i=QX_{i+1}. $$

Here the braid relation is imposed for $1\le i<n-1$ and the distant commutation relation for $1\le i,j<n$. Define the **multiplicative cyclotomic Hecke algebra of level $r$ and rank $n$** by

$$ H_{r,n}=\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{aff}}/(p(X_1)), $$

where $(p(X_1))$ denotes the two-sided ideal it generates. The unit $Q$ and the quadratic relation make every $T_i$ invertible, with $T_i^{-1}=Q^{-1}(T_i-(Q-1))$. The cyclotomic relation also gives the polynomial inverse

$$ X_1^{-1}=(-1)^{r+1}(u_1\cdots u_r)^{-1}\bigl(X_1^{r-1}-e_1X_1^{r-2}+\cdots+(-1)^{r-1}e_{r-1}\bigr), $$

where $e_k$ is the $k$th elementary symmetric polynomial in $u_1,\ldots,u_r$. The presentation already includes inverse generators; this formula records that the quotient does not require a separate inverse parameter. For $i\ge1$, write $X_{i+1}=Q^{-1}T_iX_iT_i$ when using the recursion determined by the affine relation.

This is the multiplicative presentation. It is not the additive degenerate cyclotomic presentation obtained after setting a parameter equal to $1$ and changing generators.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $R$, $v_s$, $H$, $T_s$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]; let $T_w$ for $w\in W$ and the spanning statement be as in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]]; and let $E$, $P_s$, $Q_s$ and $P_w$ be as in [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. 3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.

$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$

For $r,n\ge 1$, let $H_{r,n}$ be the multiplicative cyclotomic Hecke algebra of [[def-hh-multiplicative-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]]. There is a unique $R$-linear involutive algebra anti-automorphism $*$ of $H_{r,n}$ fixing every $T_i$ and every $X_j^{\pm1}$. Since $L_j=X_j$ by [[lem-hh-cyclotomic-commuting-jucys-murphy-generators]], it fixes every $L_j$. Its restriction to the finite type-A Hecke subalgebra is the reversal anti-involution.

An **$r$-multipartition** of $n$ is a tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(r)})$ of ordinary partitions whose total number of boxes is $n$. Its boxes are triples $(c,a,b)$ with $1\le c\le r$, $a\ge1$, and $1\le b\le\lambda^{(c)}_a$. Order the boxes within component $c$ by the transitive closure of $(c,a,b)<(c,a,b+1)$ and $(c,a,b)<(c,a+1,b)$; boxes in different components are incomparable.

A **standard multitableau** $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is a bijective filling of the boxes by $1,\ldots,n$ that increases along every row and column. Equivalently, it is a linear extension of this finite box poset. Write $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ for the set of such fillings and

$$ \operatorname{res}_t(i)=u_cQ^{b-a}\quad\text{if entry }i\text{ occupies }(c,a,b). $$

The **generic content field** is $K=\mathbb Q(Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r)$, the fraction field of $R$. The contents of distinct addable boxes of any multipartition are distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have the same content, they lie on one diagonal; the right and lower boxes immediately between them are distinct required predecessors of the southeast box. Consequently, for three consecutive labels $i,i+1,i+2$ in a standard multitableau, the first and third contents cannot agree. In particular every pair of contents among three consecutive labels is distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have content exponents differing by $1$, then they are comparable in the box order, so interchanging adjacent labels in a standard multitableau never gives a content ratio $Q$ or $Q^{-1}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a unital associative $R$-algebra. A **cell datum** for $A$ consists of a finite poset $(\Lambda,\ge)$, finite sets $T(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda$, an $R$-basis $\{C^\lambda_{s,t}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$ of $A$, and an $R$-linear involutive algebra anti-automorphism $*$ satisfying $({C^\lambda_{s,t}})^*=C^\lambda_{t,s}$ and the following coefficient-independence axiom: for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, $s,t\in T(\lambda)$, and $a\in A$, there are coefficients $r^\lambda_{t,v}(a)\in R$, independent of $s$, such that
$$C^\lambda_{s,t}a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r^\lambda_{t,v}(a)C^\lambda_{s,v}\pmod{A^{>\lambda}},$$

$$\sum_{d<c}|\lambda^{(d)}|+\sum_{i=1}^{j}\lambda_i^{(c)} \ \ge\ \sum_{d<c}|\mu^{(d)}|+\sum_{i=1}^{j}\mu_i^{(c)},$$
with missing rows padded by zero. Write $\lambda\triangleright\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\lambda\ne\mu$. The **row-standard initial multitableau** $t^\lambda$ fills component $1$ row by row, then component $2$ row by row, and so on, using $1,\ldots,n$ in order.

derivations.claim: The commuting property in [F1] makes each product in $u_\lambda$ a defined polynomial element. The presentation [F2] supplies the coefficient ring, unit parameters, and quotient in which these polynomials live. The row subgroup $S_\lambda$ is a product of finite symmetric groups on consecutive row intervals, so every $T_w$ in $x_\lambda$ is a defined finite Hecke element by [F3]. For standard $t$, the equality $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$ determines $d(t)$ uniquely because the entry action is free; row-increasing entries mean that this representative is minimal in the row-stabilizer coset, by the parabolic description in [F3]. Thus all displayed expressions are elements of $H_{r,n}$.

It remains to verify the stated commutation. Let $T_i$ generate a row factor belonging to component $k$, so $i,i+1$ lie in that component's label interval. For a factor with index $c\le k$, [F5] gives $a_c<i$, so every $L_j$ in $\prod_{j\le a_c}(L_j-u_c)$ is distant from $T_i$ and commutes with it by [F1]. For a factor with $c>k$, [F5] gives $a_c\ge i+1$, so the factor contains both $(L_i-u_c)$ and $(L_{i+1}-u_c)$; the entire product over $j\le a_c$ is invariant under swapping $L_i,L_{i+1}$. The divided-difference term in [F1] is then zero, and [F1] gives commutation with $T_i$. Therefore $u_\lambda$ commutes with every generator of $S_\lambda$, hence with every $T_w$ in that group and with their sum $x_\lambda$.

Since the row subgroup is closed under inversion, $x_\lambda^*=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_{w^{-1}}=x_\lambda$. Also $u_\lambda^*=u_\lambda$ by [F4]. The commutation proved in step 2.1 gives $m_\lambda^*=(u_\lambda x_\lambda)^*=x_\lambda u_\lambda=u_\lambda x_\lambda=m_\lambda$. Applying the anti-involution to the defining formula for $m_{st}$ now yields $m_{st}^*=T_{d(t)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

derivations.claim: Put $R'_A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and map $R_A\to R'_A$ by $Q\mapsto v^2$. Every Laurent polynomial in $v$ has a unique expression $f(Q)+vg(Q)$, so $R'_A$ is free over $R_A$ on $1,v$ and $R_A\hookrightarrow R'_A$. In the symmetric normalization of [F1], setting $T_i=v\widetilde T_i$ gives $(T_i-v^2)(T_i+1)=0$ and preserves braid relations; the generator rescaling multiplies $T_w$ by the unit $v^{\ell(w)}$. Thus the base-changed algebra over $R'_A$ has basis $\{T_w\}$ by [F1]. The quadratic relation spans products over $R_A$; any relation among the $T_w$ remains a relation over $R'_A$, where they are independent. Injectivity of $R_A\to R'_A$ proves that $\{T_w\}$ is an $R_A$-basis.

For a composition $\alpha$, let $x_\alpha=\sum_{w\in S_\alpha}T_w$. The elements $x_\alpha T_d$ for distinguished right coset representatives $d$ span $x_\alpha H_n$ because each group element factors uniquely as $yd$ with $y\in S_\alpha$ and $\ell(yd)=\ell(y)+\ell(d)$, while $x_\alpha T_y=Q^{\ell(y)}x_\alpha$. Their standard-basis supports are disjoint cosets and each has coefficient $1$ at its distinguished representative, so they are independent. If $s_i$ is a row generator, pairing $w$ and $ws_i$ in $x_\alpha T_i$ and using the two Hecke multiplication cases gives $x_\alpha T_i=Qx_\alpha$. Consequently, on the row-module basis $e_t=x_\alpha T_{d(t)}$, multiplication by $T_i$ has the three cases: $Qe_t$ if $ts_i$ is not row standard, $e_{ts_i}$ if it is row standard and length increases, and $Qe_{ts_i}+(Q-1)e_t$ if it is row standard and length decreases. The left-action formulas follow by applying $*$.

Define $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$. The two Hecke multiplication cases give $\tau(T_wT_i)=\tau(T_iT_w)=Q\delta_{w,s_i}$; moving the generator letters of a word around the trace one at a time therefore proves $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for arbitrary $a,b$. Define $B(T_u,T_v)=\delta_{u,v}Q^{\ell(u)}$. On each right-$s_i$ pair with $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1$, right multiplication has matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q\\1&Q-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B$ has matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(Q^{\ell(w)},Q^{\ell(w)+1})$; direct multiplication gives $A^{\mathsf T}D=DA$. Distinct pairs are orthogonal, hence $B(aT_i,b)=B(a,bT_i)$. Moving the letters of a reduced word for $u$ from the first argument to the second now gives $B(T_u,T_v)=\tau(T_vT_u^*)=\tau(T_u^*T_v)$. Thus $\tau(a^*b)$ is a unimodular pairing: its standard-basis Gram matrix is diagonal with the units $Q^{\ell(w)}$. The pairing $\tau(ab)$ is also unimodular, since $*$ permutes the standard basis.

For $\alpha$ a composition and $\bar\alpha$ the partition obtained by sorting its parts, reorder the consecutive row blocks by a permutation $d$ so that $S_\alpha d=dS_{\bar\alpha}$. The blocks are intervals, so the intersections of the two block decompositions are intervals; parabolic length additivity gives $x_\alpha T_d=T_dx_{\bar\alpha}$ and hence $x_\alpha=T_dx_{\bar\alpha}T_d^{-1}$. The row-module bases from step 2.1 show that $Hx_{\bar\alpha}H$ is spanned by row-standard Murphy elements of partition shape $\bar\alpha$. Thus every row-standard Murphy element of composition shape $\alpha$ lies in that span.

Fix $\lambda\vdash n$ and a node $(i,j)$ with $\lambda_{i+1}\ge j$. Set $a=t^\lambda(i,j)$, $b=t^\lambda(i+1,j)$, and let $g$ be the Garnir tableau that fills the belt (row $i$ from column $j$ to its end and row $i+1$ from its start through column $j$) increasingly, first along the lower row segment and then along the upper segment. Put $

The tableaux $t^\lambda w$ on the left consist of $g$ and the tableaux obtained by assigning any other $j$-element subset of belt labels to the lower segment; those are standard and strictly more dominant than $g$, since at the first label where the subset differs, a smaller label moves to the upper row. Isolating the $g$ term expresses $x_\lambda T_{d(g)}$ as a linear combination of row-standard Murphy elements of shape $

Let $t$ be a nonstandard row-standard $\lambda$-tableau and choose a column violation $t(i,j)>t(i+1,j)$. Order the boxes first by row order and add the relation $(i+1,j)<(i,j)$. Both $t$ and the Garnir tableau $g$ of step 4.1 are linear extensions. The inversions of $g$ relative to row reading are exactly the pairs consisting of a lower-belt box through column $j$ followed by an upper-belt box from column $j$ onward; the added relation and the two row orders force every such pair in every extension. Thus the inversion set of $g$ is contained in that of $t$. For row-standard tableaux the Coxeter length of $d(t)$ counts these inversions, and $t=g\cdot w$ for the relative permutation $w$ has $\ell(w)$ equal to the number of pairs whose order differs between $g$ and $t$. For fixed shape, define tableau dominance by comparing, for every label cutoff $m$ and row cutoff $k$, the number of entries at most $m$ in the first $k$ rows. This relation agrees with Bruhat order on the distinguished permutations: at row boundaries the Bruhat rank numbers are exactly these counts by [F7]; inside a row, row standardness makes the count the minimum of the preceding-row count plus the partial row length and the count at the next row boundary, so boundary inequalities give all rank inequalities. Hence $u\triangleright_{\rm tab}t$ implies $d(u)<d(t)$. In step 4.1, each standard tableau $u\triangleright_{\rm tab}g$ has $d(u)$ a proper reduced subword of $d(g)$. Multiplying its row-module element by the reduced word $T_w$ of step 5.1, every standard-basis term is represented by a subword of the reduced expression for $d(t)=d(g)w$. Parabolic reduction to its distinguished row representative preserves the subword inequality. Thus all same-shape output tableaux strictly dominate $t$. Induction first on the finite lexicographic shape order and then on the finite tableau order, and applying $*$ for the first index, straightens every row-standard Murphy element to standard Murphy elements; higher-shape terms are handled before lower shapes.

When $\lambda=(1^n)$, $x_\lambda=1$ and the row-standard elements include every standard Hecke basis element $T_w$. Step 6.1 therefore shows that the standard Murphy elements span $H_n$. Their number is $\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$ by [F3], equal to the rank of $H_n$ by step 1.1. The square coordinate matrix of this spanning family has a right inverse, hence unit determinant by [F4], so the Murphy elements form an $R_A$-basis. For $x_\lambda h\in x_\lambda H_n$, the row-module basis and step 6.1 express it modulo higher lexicographic shapes as $\sum_v r_vx_\lambda T_{d(v)}$, with coefficients independent of a later first tableau.
